planning.title: The planning catch that trips people up in Harlow
paragraphs: Here is the thing worth knowing before you sketch anything, because a lot of Harlow homeowners get caught out by it.

Harlow has Article 4 directions covering parts of the town, including Old Harlow, Mark Hall North and Morley Grove. In plain English, an Article 4 direction removes permitted development rights you would normally have, so work that would be automatic on the next street can need a full planning application on yours.

On top of that, Harlow has ten conservation areas. Some are the historic bits you would expect, like Old Harlow and Churchgate Street. Others are more surprising: Mark Hall North was designated to protect the architecture of the New Town itself, being the first neighbourhood Gibberd completed. If you live in one, design and materials get looked at more closely.

Away from those areas, plenty of Harlow homes keep normal permitted development rights and a well-sized extension can go ahead without an application at all. The point is simply that it varies street by street here more than in most towns, and assuming you are covered when you are not is an expensive mistake. We check your address with Harlow Council before anything is drawn, and handle the application if one is needed.

ground.title: The ground under Harlow
paragraphs: Harlow sits on boulder clay over London Clay, on ground that rises from the Stort valley in the north up to the higher land in the south. Gibberd deliberately built on the high ground and left the valleys open, which is one reason the town itself has largely avoided serious flooding.

The clay is the thing that matters for your foundations. It swells in the wet and shrinks in dry spells, and it moves most near mature trees, of which Harlow's green wedges and parks give you plenty. On a leafy plot, foundations often need to go deeper than people expect, and closer to the Stort the ground softens. We check the ground early and, on trickier plots, get it properly investigated before pricing the groundworks.

cost.title: What an extension costs in Harlow
paragraphs: Cost comes down to size, specification, structural work and finish, plus any material matching on an older home.

As a rough guide, single-storey extensions commonly run at a few thousand pounds per square metre, with double storey often better value per square metre. That is a starting point, not a quote. Our cost calculator gives an early estimate, and a free site visit gives you a real, itemised figure.

faqs.q: What is an Article 4 direction, and does it affect my Harlow home?
faqs.a: An Article 4 direction removes permitted development rights that homeowners normally have, meaning you need planning permission for work that would otherwise be automatic. In Harlow they apply to areas including Old Harlow, Mark Hall North and Morley Grove. We check whether yours is affected before you plan anything.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission for an extension in Harlow?
faqs.a: It genuinely depends on your street. Away from the Article 4 areas and the town's ten conservation areas, many homes keep normal permitted development rights and can extend without a full application. Inside them, more work needs permission. We confirm your position with Harlow Council and handle any application.

faqs.q: Is Mark Hall North really a conservation area?
faqs.a: Yes, and it surprises people. It was designated to protect the architecture of the New Town itself, as the first neighbourhood completed under Gibberd's plan, so its original housing styles and features are protected in the same way an old high street would be.

faqs.q: Why does the local ground matter for my foundations?
faqs.a: Harlow sits on boulder clay over London Clay, which moves with the seasons and shifts most near large trees, and this is a leafy town. That often means deeper foundations than expected, so we check the ground before pricing rather than meeting it mid-build.
